title: Paper 1 Question 1: Comprehension
description: How to attack the 20-mark comprehension question on Text A: explicit versus implicit meaning, reading the mark tariff, choosing precise evidence, and pacing yourself across the paper.

notes.heading: The Shape of Question 1
notes.body: Question 1 Comprehension is worth 20 marks on Text A, the first of the three texts. You answer a series of short-answer sub-questions of different lengths and mark tariffs, writing in the spaces provided on the question paper — there is no choice of questions. For 2027–2029 it tests all five reading objectives (R1 to R5), so although most sub-questions ask you to find or explain meanings, later parts may ask you to develop ideas, comment on effects, or select details for a stated purpose. Read each sub-question's command word before you answer: 'identify' or 'give' wants a phrase; 'explain' wants a point plus its why or how, supported from the text. Budget about 30 of the paper's 120 minutes here, including your share of the 15 minutes' reading time — the paper averages roughly 1.5 minutes per mark once reading is folded in.

notes.heading: Explicit Meaning (R1): Retrieval with Precision
notes.body: An explicit meaning is stated directly in the text — you retrieve it, you do not infer it. Example: 'The ferry left the harbour at six, although the sky was already darkening.' Explicit facts include: the ferry left at six; the sky was darkening. Anything beyond that — the crossing will be rough, the crew is worried — is inference, not retrieval. Technique: find the relevant lines, then answer in a short phrase or sentence that contains only what was asked. Two traps cost marks. First, answering from your own assumption or general knowledge instead of the text — the examiner can only reward what the passage supports. Second, burying the answer: copying a whole sentence when the question asked for one detail forces the marker to hunt for it, and any wrong extra detail can contradict an otherwise correct point.

notes.heading: Implicit Meaning (R2): Reading Between the Lines
notes.body: Implicit meaning is suggested rather than stated, and attitudes almost always live here. Writers signal feelings through word choice, tone, what they emphasise and what they leave out. Example: 'Marta smiled at the interviewer, folded her hands twice, and answered each question about her resignation in fewer than five words.' Nothing says Marta is uncomfortable — but the repeated hand-folding and the clipped answers signal someone guarded and reluctant. The method is a two-step: first decide what the detail makes you think (the inference), then name the words that create that impression (the anchor). An inference with no anchor is a guess; an anchor with no inference is just quotation. You need both, in that order.

illustration.alt: A short passage with two phrases highlighted: a directly stated fact labelled explicit meaning, and word choices that suggest an attitude without stating it, labelled implicit meaning.
illustration.caption: Explicit meaning is stated in the words; implicit meaning is signalled by them. Strong answers give the inference and anchor it to the words that create it.

notes.heading: The Mark Tariff Is an Instruction
notes.body: The number in brackets tells you exactly how much to write. One mark means one clear point — a phrase or a sentence. Two marks means two distinct points, or one point plus development (the point, then 'because…' or 'which shows…'). Three or four marks means that many distinct, developed points, usually with textual support. Two failure patterns follow. Over-answering: five lines for a 1-mark question spends time you owe to later questions and adds nothing. Under-answering: five words for a 4-mark question cannot contain four points no matter how well phrased. Get in the habit of checking the tariff twice — before you answer, so you know the target, and after, counting whether you have actually made as many distinct points as there are marks. Writing the same point twice in different words is still one point.

notes.heading: Choosing and Using Evidence
notes.body: Where a sub-question asks you to support or develop (R3), the skill is selection. Pick the shortest quotation that proves your point — typically two to six words — and integrate it into your own sentence: 'The writer presents the sea as violent: it clawed at the hull.' Quote only when the wording itself carries the meaning; otherwise paraphrase. An over-long quotation smuggles in irrelevant words and tells the marker you have not selected. Know which question you are in: Question 1 rewards precise, well-anchored evidence, while Question 2(a) demands your own words, so a habit of lifting phrases costs you writing marks there. And never let a quotation contradict your point — a mismatched quote loses both the reading mark and the marker's confidence.

notes.heading: Pacing and Process Across the Paper
notes.body: The paper starts with about 15 minutes of reading: three texts, roughly 1400 words in total. Read actively — underline facts, circle words that carry attitude, and note where a text changes direction. Then work the questions in order; the sub-questions of Question 1 are sequenced through Text A, so earlier answers often orient you for later ones. The arithmetic is simple: four equally-weighted questions in 120 minutes is about 30 minutes each, with the 15 minutes of reading folded into the questions you spend it on — that is roughly 1.5 minutes per mark once reading is included, so about 30 minutes for Question 1. If a sub-question stalls you, write what you can and move on; a blank is guaranteed zero, while the next sub-question is fresh marks. Keep two minutes at the end of the question to re-check each answer against its tariff.

notes.heading: Failure Modes That Cost Marks
notes.body: Six habits account for most lost comprehension marks. Retelling: narrating what happens in the text instead of answering the question asked. Feature-spotting: naming a simile or an example of alliteration without explaining its meaning — technique labels are not understanding. The quotation dump: copying three lines and hoping the answer is in there somewhere. Answering from your head: giving your own opinion or knowledge where the question asks about the text. Ignoring 'in your own words' where it appears: lifted phrases cannot be credited there. And double-counting: writing one point twice and expecting two marks. Each of these feels productive in the moment and scores badly against a mark scheme. The fix for all six is the same discipline: answer the exact question, at the depth the tariff demands, with evidence you have actually selected. To build the skill, practise with this course's free-response sets and AI marking; the quiz here trains the judgement.

flashcards.definition: A meaning stated directly in the text; tested by R1. Retrieved, not inferred.
flashcards.example: 'The ferry left the harbour at six' — the departure time is stated, so finding it is an R1 task.

flashcards.definition: A meaning suggested but not stated; tested by R2. Inferred from word choice, tone, emphasis and omission.
flashcards.example: A character who 'folded her hands twice' and answered in five words is guarded — the text never says so.

flashcards.definition: A conclusion drawn from textual evidence; strong answers state the inference and anchor it to the words that create it.
flashcards.example: 'He is nervous (inference) — his hands would not stay still (anchor).'

flashcards.definition: The marks available for a sub-question, which dictate depth: 1 mark = one point; 2 or more marks = multiple points or point plus development.
flashcards.example: A 4-mark 'explain' question needs four distinct supported points, not one point written four ways.

flashcards.definition: For 2-mark questions: make the point, then add why or how — 'because…' or 'which shows…'.
flashcards.example: 'The journey was dangerous (point) because the sea clawed at the hull all night (development).'

flashcards.definition: The shortest quotation that proves the point — usually two to six words — integrated into your own sentence.
flashcards.example: The writer makes the sea violent: it 'clawed at the hull'.

flashcards.definition: Restating the text's idea in your own words; preferred unless the exact wording carries the meaning, and essential where 'own words' is required.
flashcards.example: Text: 'the town's lights shrank behind the swell' → paraphrase: 'the town disappeared from view'.

flashcards.definition: Narrating what happens in the text instead of answering the question — shows no selection and earns little credit.
flashcards.example: Recounting the whole crossing when asked what the narrator feared about it.

flashcards.definition: The writer's or speaker's feelings and views, usually signalled implicitly through word choice and tone (R2).
flashcards.example: Calling a plan 'interesting' while studying your shoes signals scepticism, not enthusiasm.

flashcards.definition: Annotating during the 15-minute reading time: underline facts, circle attitude words, mark shifts in direction.
flashcards.example: Circling 'reluctantly', 'at last' and 'thankfully' before any question is read.

flashcards.definition: Select and use information for specific purposes — some Question 1 sub-questions ask you to pick out details for a stated purpose.
flashcards.example: 'Give two details that show the harbour was busy' — only details serving that purpose score.

flashcards.definition: About 1.5 minutes per mark, reading time included: roughly 30 minutes for Question 1 inside the 2-hour paper.
flashcards.example: Spending 40 minutes on Question 1 borrows 10 minutes from Questions 2 to 4.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'The bus arrived forty minutes late, its wipers scraping across a dry windscreen.' Which statement is an explicit meaning?
choices: The bus company was badly managed
The bus arrived forty minutes late
The passengers were furious
The driver was inexperienced
questions.explanation: Only the late arrival is stated directly in the sentence, so it is the explicit meaning (R1). Bad management, furious passengers and an inexperienced driver are all guesses — nothing in the sentence states or signals them, so treating any of them as fact is inference without an anchor.

questions.stem: A sub-question carries 4 marks. Which response plan fits the tariff?
choices: One point explained at great length
Two points plus a long quotation
A single precise sentence, to show economy
Four distinct points, each briefly supported or developed
questions.explanation: A 4-mark tariff demands four distinct creditable points, each developed or supported. One point at any length is still one point; two points plus a quotation tops out around half the marks; and a single sentence cannot physically contain four points however precise it is.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'Leo described the new timetable as "interesting", then spent the rest of the meeting studying his shoes.' Which inference about Leo's attitude is BEST supported?
choices: He is sceptical — the hollow praise of 'interesting' combined with avoiding eye contact signals doubt
He is fascinated by the timetable and wants to study it further
He dislikes meetings in general
He is simply shy around colleagues
questions.explanation: The quotation marks around 'interesting' and the shoe-studying both point to withheld approval, so scepticism is the inference anchored in the text. Fascination contradicts the body language. Disliking meetings and being shy are possible in life but unsupported here — the text ties his behaviour to this specific announcement, and R2 rewards only what the words signal.

questions.stem: What does the reading objective R2 test?
choices: Understanding of explicit meanings
Analysing and evaluating ideas with textual support
Understanding of implicit meanings and attitudes
Selecting information for a specific purpose
questions.explanation: R2 is implicit meanings and attitudes — what the text suggests rather than states. Explicit meaning is R1, analysing and evaluating with support is R3, and selecting for a purpose is R5; confusing these leads to retrieval answers where inference was asked for.

questions.stem: A question asks for evidence that conditions were severe. The text reads: 'Rain hammered the tent all night, and by dawn the field had become a slow brown river.' Which is the most economical quotation that still proves the severity?
choices: 'by dawn'
'hammered'
'Rain hammered the tent all night, and by dawn the field had become a slow brown river'
'the field had become a slow brown river'
questions.explanation: 'Hammered' is the shortest quotation that carries the severity — a violent verb, two syllables, fully integrated. 'By dawn' says nothing about severity. The whole sentence smuggles in irrelevant material and shows no selection, and the 'slow brown river' clause, while relevant, is a long image where one word does the job — strong evidence is precise, not large.

questions.stem: A student answers a 2-mark 'explain' question with: 'The writer feels nostalgic. The writer says the house smelled of cinnamon.' What must be added to earn the second mark?
choices: A definition of the word 'nostalgic'
A longer quotation about the house
Nothing — a point plus a quotation is already two points
Development linking the evidence to the feeling — for example, that the smell of cinnamon recalls childhood kitchens, so the detail awakens warm memory
questions.explanation: The answer has a point and an anchor but no link between them; the second mark comes from explaining how the evidence produces the feeling. Defining 'nostalgic' adds no textual understanding, a longer quotation is selection getting worse not better, and a point plus a bare quotation is only one developed unit — without the link, the development mark is missing.

questions.stem: How long does the syllabus advise spending on reading the three Paper 1 texts before you start writing?
choices: About 15 minutes
About 45 minutes
About 3 minutes — skim and start
No reading time is built into the paper
questions.explanation: The syllabus advises about 15 minutes reading the three texts, which total roughly 1400 words. Forty-five minutes would consume over a third of the paper, three minutes is too little to annotate anything, and reading time is explicitly recommended — it is part of how the 2 hours is meant to be used.

questions.stem: A sub-question ends with 'in your own words'. What changes about your answer?
choices: You should quote more, to prove you read the text
Nothing — quotation is always acceptable
You must paraphrase — lifted phrases cannot be credited
You must write at least 120 words
questions.explanation: 'In your own words' makes paraphrase a condition of credit: copied phrases are excluded from the answer. Quoting more makes things worse, not better; the instruction plainly changes the rules, so 'nothing changes' fails; and the 120-word figure is the limit for Question 2(a)'s summary, not a requirement here.

questions.stem: The text says: 'The council planted two hundred saplings along the verge in March.' For the sub-question 'Identify when the saplings were planted [1]', which answer is strongest?
choices: 'The council planted two hundred saplings along the verge in March.'
'In March.'
'A long time ago, in the spring.'
'Two hundred saplings.'
questions.explanation: 'In March.' is the precise answer to a 1-mark 'identify' question — one point, nothing else. Copying the whole sentence buries the answer and wastes time; 'a long time ago, in the spring' is vague and replaces a stated fact with a weaker paraphrase; and 'two hundred saplings' answers how many, not when, so it misses the question entirely.

questions.stem: Why does retelling the story score badly in comprehension answers?
choices: Retold answers are usually too short
Retelling uses too few quotations
Retelling only loses marks in Question 4
It shows no selection and no engagement with what the question asked — marks reward answers, not proof that you read the text
questions.explanation: Comprehension marks reward answers to the specific question at the tariff's depth; narrating events demonstrates neither selection nor understanding of the demand. Length and quotation count are not the issue — a retold paragraph can be long and heavily quoted and still score almost nothing, and the habit loses marks in every question, not just Question 4.

questions.stem: A 1-mark sub-question should be answered with…
choices: one clear, precise point
a full paragraph with two quotations
at least three developed points
a quotation of several lines
questions.explanation: One mark buys one point: a phrase or single sentence. A paragraph, three points or a multi-line quotation all overspend time that is owed to later, higher-tariff questions — and the extra material can never earn more than the single mark on offer.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: '"Of course," said Priya, "a three-hour meeting about punctuality was exactly what the day needed."' Which reading of Priya's attitude is best?
choices: She is genuinely grateful the meeting was held
She is angry about the punctuality rules themselves
She is being ironic — 'of course' and 'exactly what the day needed' mean the opposite, mocking the meeting's absurdity
She is bored with her job in general
questions.explanation: A three-hour meeting about punctuality is inherently absurd, so 'of course' and 'exactly what the day needed' work ironically — the words say one thing and mean the opposite. Gratitude takes the words literally, the classic R2 error. The text mocks the meeting, not punctuality rules, and boredom with her whole job over-generalises from one event.

questions.stem: Question 1 Comprehension is based on which text, and how many marks does it carry?
choices: Text B; 20 marks
Text C; 10 marks
Text A; 20 marks
All three texts; 20 marks
questions.explanation: Question 1 responds to Text A and is worth 20 marks, like every Paper 1 question. Text B belongs to Question 2, Text C to Questions 3 and 4, and each question targets its own text rather than all three.

questions.stem: You notice you have spent 40 minutes on Question 1. What is the best move?
choices: Wrap up within a couple of minutes and move on — at about 1.5 minutes per mark, 20 marks should take about 30 minutes, and the extra time is being borrowed from later questions
Keep polishing — Question 1 is the most important question on the paper
Stop mid-sentence and never return to it
Skip reading the later texts to compensate — you can answer from the questions alone
questions.explanation: At roughly 1.5 minutes per mark, Question 1's 20 marks are budgeted at about 30 minutes, so 40 minutes means you are overspending; finish the current sub-question and move on. All four questions carry equal marks, so Question 1 is not the most important. Never abandon an answer mid-sentence — partial credit counts. And skipping the reading guarantees weak answers later; the texts must be read.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'The writer uses a metaphor in line 12 and alliteration in line 15.' Why does this score poorly in a sub-question about what the narrator finds frightening?
choices: Metaphors are not allowed in comprehension answers
Line references should never be included
It should have listed more techniques to cover the marks
It names features without saying what they mean — technique labels are not understanding, and neither label answers what the narrator finds frightening
questions.explanation: Feature-spotting names devices but never engages with meaning, so it cannot answer a question about what frightens the narrator. Metaphors and line references are perfectly acceptable when tied to meaning; and listing more techniques would multiply the same error, not fix it — one explained effect outscores five unexplained labels.
